claims.text: Stability of a single-phase solid solution in high-entropy alloy nanoparticles over 473–1923 K is primarily governed by the interplay between initial lattice strain and temperature-accelerated atomic diffusion.
Nanoparticles with higher initial lattice strain undergo faster atomic diffusion at elevated temperatures.
Faster atomic diffusion in highly strained nanoparticles produces strain relief.
Strain relief through accelerated atomic rearrangement leads to phase segregation.
Strain relief through accelerated atomic rearrangement leads to chemical reordering.
Nanoparticles with lower initial lattice strain have slower diffusion kinetics and remain stable as a solid solution.
HEA solid solutions exhibit measurable local lattice strain.
The magnitude of local lattice strain influences the rate of atomic diffusion and rearrangement within a nanoparticle.
Higher pre-existing lattice strain creates localized dislocations.
Localized dislocations enhance atomic diffusion under thermal stress.
Elevated temperature can induce structural transformations in solid materials.
Under prolonged high-temperature dwell, initially high-strain nanoparticles will develop more secondary phases than low-strain nanoparticles.
Under prolonged high-temperature dwell, initially high-strain nanoparticles will develop greater chemical inhomogeneity than low-strain nanoparticles.
The predicted strain-dependent instability requires a heating profile and dwell time that permit significant atomic diffusion.
Nanoparticle size can modify the proposed strain-dependent stability behavior.
The ambient environment can modify the proposed strain-dependent stability behavior.
The critical lattice-strain and dwell-time values for destabilization vary with particle size and elemental composition.
